topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Biology — Biota and Environment — 2024
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What are biotic and abiotic components of the environment? Give two examples of each.
questions.solution:
**Biotic** (living): plants, animals, microbes — producers, consumers, decomposers.

**Abiotic** (non-living): light, temperature, water, soil, air, minerals — the stage every organism performs on.
questions.knowledgeNote: Liebig's law of the minimum: the scarcest factor limits growth, however abundant the rest.
questions.answer: **Abiotic components:** the **non-living physical and chemical factors** of an ecosystem — e.g. **light, temperature, water, soil/minerals, air (CO₂, O₂), humidity, pH**. **Biotic components:** the **living organisms** of the ecosystem, classified by function into **producers (green plants), consumers (animals — herbivores, carnivores, omnivores), and decomposers (bacteria, fungi)**. **Two examples of each:** abiotic — **sunlight and rainfall** (or soil, temperature); biotic — **grass (producer) and cow (consumer)** (or bacteria as decomposers). **Deep point:** the two component classes are the ecosystem's two halves — matter and energy flow through both, but only the biotic half can *use* the energy and only the abiotic half can *supply* it.

questions.question: What are hydrophytes and xerophytes? Write two adaptive features of each.
questions.solution:
**Hydrophytes** (water plants, e.g. lotus): aerenchyma air spaces for buoyancy, waxy waterproof leaves, reduced roots.

**Xerophytes** (dry-land plants, e.g. cactus): fleshy water-storing stems, spines instead of leaves, sunken stomata and thick cuticle against transpiration.
questions.knowledgeNote: Opposite water problems, opposite engineering — environment sculpts anatomy predictably.
questions.answer: **Hydrophytes:** plants adapted to **life in water or waterlogged soil** (e.g. **water hyacinth, lotus (*Nelumbo*), *Hydrilla*, water lily**). **Two adaptive features:** (1) **thin cuticle, poorly developed xylem** — water is never scarce, so support and water-transport tissue are reduced; soft stems kept buoyant by **aerenchyma** (air-filled spaces); (2) **broad floating leaves with stomata only on the upper surface** (or finely divided submerged leaves) to maximise gas exchange. **Xerophytes:** plants adapted to **dry, water-scarce habitats** (deserts, rocks; e.g. **cactus (*Opuntia*), *Aloe*, *Casuarina*, acacia**). **Two adaptive features:** (1) **thick cuticle, sunken stomata, leaves reduced to spines** — minimising water loss; photosynthesis taken over by the succulent stem (CAM metabolism in cacti); (2) **extensive, deep root systems and water-storing succulent tissues** — maximising uptake and storage. **Deep point:** the two groups are mirror strategies — hydrophytes throw away the water-conservation machinery, xerophytes build more of it; every feature answers one question: 'how much water can I afford to lose?'

questions.question: Define natality, mortality, and population density. How are they related to population growth?
questions.solution:
**Natality** (birth rate) adds; **mortality** (death rate) subtracts; **density** (individuals per unit area) is the current stock.

Growth = (natality + immigration) − (mortality + emigration) — density rises only when arrivals beat departures.
questions.knowledgeNote: J-shaped (exponential) vs S-shaped (logistic, carrying capacity K) — the two growth curves behind every population question.
questions.answer: **Natality (birth rate):** the number of **individuals born per unit time** in a population (often per 1000 individuals per year) — the only process that adds individuals by birth/germination. **Mortality (death rate):** the number of **individuals dying per unit time** — the process removing individuals. **Population density:** the **number of individuals per unit area or volume** (e.g. deer per km²) — the fundamental measure of population size. **Relation to population growth:** population growth is the **balance sheet of four processes** — **growth = (natality + immigration) − (mortality + emigration)**. When natality exceeds mortality the population grows; when mortality exceeds natality it shrinks; when they are equal, density stays stable. Natality and mortality are therefore the two levers that directly drive density change. **Deep point:** the growth equation has four terms but two directions — births and immigration push up, deaths and emigration push down; a population's future is just which pair is winning.

questions.question: What are the major causes and effects of air pollution?
questions.solution:
**Causes:** vehicle exhaust (CO, NOₓ), brick kilns and industry (SPM, SO₂), biomass burning, dust from construction.

**Effects:** respiratory disease, acid rain, smog cutting visibility, greenhouse warming; Kathmandu's winter inversion traps it all into hazardous AQI weeks.
questions.knowledgeNote: Kathmandu Valley's bowl topography + winter inversion = Nepal's own air-pollution case study.
questions.answer: **Major causes of air pollution:** (1) **combustion of fossil fuels** — vehicles, industries, brick kilns and power plants releasing CO, CO₂, SO₂, NOₓ and particulates (in Nepal: old vehicles, brick kilns, unpaved roads); (2) **burning of biomass and waste** — crop residue, firewood smoke, open waste burning; (3) **industrial and construction dust** — cement dust, road dust, PM10/PM2.5; (4) **indoor pollution** — smoke from traditional biomass stoves. **Effects:** (1) **respiratory and cardiac disease** — PM2.5 penetrates deep into lungs (asthma, bronchitis, reduced life expectancy; Kathmandu's air regularly exceeds WHO guidelines); (2) **acid rain** — SO₂ and NOₓ form acids that damage crops, forests, buildings and water bodies; (3) **smog and reduced visibility** — photochemical smog, loss of Himalaya views, flight disruptions; (4) **global warming** — CO₂ and other greenhouse gases drive climate change; damage to plants and materials. **Deep point:** the same combustion event emits two kinds of harm — local toxins (CO, PM) that poison lungs today and global gases (CO₂) that warm the planet for decades; one chimney, two clocks.

questions.question: What is BOD? Why is high BOD harmful for aquatic life?
questions.solution:
**Biochemical Oxygen Demand** is the oxygen microbes consume decomposing organic matter in water (mg/L over 5 days at 20°C).

High BOD means the water's oxygen is being eaten — fish suffocate, clean-water species vanish, and only pollution-tolerant worms survive.
questions.knowledgeNote: BOD < 5 ppm is clean; Bagmati sewage stretches run far above — a number that tells a river's whole story.
questions.answer: **BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand):** the **amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms while decomposing the organic matter in a water sample** over a standard period (5 days at 20 °C) — a direct measure of how much organic pollution the water carries; clean water has BOD < 1–2 mg/L, sewage runs into the hundreds. **Why high BOD is harmful:** a high BOD means a huge microbial demand on the water's dissolved oxygen — the microbes **strip the oxygen out of the water**, and once DO falls below ~4–5 mg/L, **fish and other aerobic aquatic life suffocate and die**; the water turns septic, anaerobic bacteria take over, producing foul-smelling H₂S, and the ecosystem collapses. **Deep point:** BOD is an oxygen bill — the organic matter is the debt, dissolved oxygen the currency, and fish are the first creditors to go unpaid.

questions.question: What is soil erosion? Suggest any three conservation measures practised in Nepal.
questions.solution:
**Soil erosion** is the removal of topsoil by water and wind — Nepal's hills lose tonnes per hectare yearly.

**Measures:** (1) terrace farming on slopes; (2) community-forest afforestation stabilising catchments; (3) check dams and contour bunding slowing runoff.
questions.knowledgeNote: Community forestry now covers a third of Nepal's forest — devolved conservation that reversed Himalayan deforestation.
questions.answer: **Soil erosion:** the **removal of the fertile topsoil by agents such as water (rain, rills, gullies, landslides) and wind**, accelerated far beyond natural rates by deforestation, overgrazing, steep-slope farming and construction — Nepal's steep fragile Himalayan slopes make it especially vulnerable. **Three conservation measures practised in Nepal:** (1) **community forestry and afforestation** — handing forests to user groups and replanting denuded slopes (community forests now cover a large share of national forest); (2) **terrace farming and contour bunding on slopes** — terracing slows runoff and holds soil on hillsides (plus slash-and-burn control); (3) **bio-engineering and check dams** — planting grasses/trees (e.g. *Amriso* broom grass, alder) on landslide-prone slopes, gabion/check dams in gullies and river-training works; (also: cover cropping, controlled grazing, agroforestry). **Deep point:** topsoil is centuries in the making and one monsoon in the losing — the measures all work one way: slow the water down, cover the ground, put roots in the slope.
